title: Private VPC networking deep dive - Aurelius Health
summary: Deep dive on private VPC deployment options for Redwood Private: networking patterns (PrivateLink vs VPC peering), NAT/egress, subnets, DNS resolution for model endpoints, and security requirements (KMS, audit logs). Agreed to run a benchmark in customer's VPC and share detailed architecture diagram and security whitepaper.
topics: NAT and Egress for model downloads
Subnet sizing and placement of inference nodes
DNS and Private DNS for endpoint discovery
KV cache & batching implications on networking
transcript:
[00:00] Lila Park: Alright thanks everyone for joining, I'm Lila from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. We'll jump into a deep dive on private VPC networking and runtime implications. Marco from infra will run the guts.
[00:18] Marco Rivera: hey all, yeah hi, I'll start with a quick overview of deployment patterns, then we can go into specifics like PrivateLink, NAT, subnets.
[00:30] Priya Menon: thanks, our timeline is tight, we need a POC in the next 3 weeks, and security will require SOC2 artifacts and our KMS integration.
[00:40] Hannah Li: yep, and we need to understand how keys are handled, we prefer customer-managed KMS and no plaintext model weights leaving our VPC.
[00:50] Marco Rivera: totally, so for Redwood Private we support two main connectivity patterns: AWS PrivateLink-style interface endpoints back to Redwood control plane for management, and fully private deployments where the whole runtime sits inside your VPC (customer-managed).
[01:12] Tom Becker: can you expand on the PrivateLink option? we're worried about cross-account traffic and egress.
[01:20] Marco Rivera: sure--PrivateLink gives you a stable ENI/endpoint in your VPC that talks to Redwood control plane over the AWS network. Control plane calls (rollouts, metrics, tracing) flow over that interface; inference traffic can either stay within your VPC if you host the runtime there, or go out to Redwood's dedicated hosts if you choose hosted model. Important to note: PrivateLink endpoints are regional and require route table and security group adjustments.
[01:44] Ben Carter: for inference we definitely want the runtime inside our VPC, latency is critical for a subset of endpoints. If the runtime lives in our VPC, what is the flow for model artifact downloads and quantized images?
[01:56] Marco Rivera: good question. Model artifacts are pulled during node provisioning. We support two artifact distribution modes: S3 pull via VPC endpoints (s3 gateway or s3 interface) or pre-baked AMIs/container images with model artifacts baked in. For quantized weights we often recommend pre-pulling into an EBS volume in a private subnet during init to avoid runtime cold starts.
[02:20] Priya Menon: how do we handle patching and image updates without opening wide egress? we have strict outbound controls.
[02:28] Lila Park: common pattern is to allow limited egress to Redwood's artifact S3 bucket via an S3 VPC endpoint with a restrictive bucket policy, or use a private ECR replication setup. We also support an air-gapped package delivered to your team if needed.
[02:45] Hannah Li: KMS? we need CMK integration and HSM-backed keys for model encryption keys.
[02:52] Marco Rivera: we integrate with customer KMS for encrypting model keys at rest. For HSM-level, we can support BYOK with HSM-backed CMKs; runtime attests and retrieves keys over mTLS to the KMS endpoint using an IAM role. There are steps to ensure the nodes never see plaintext keys in persistent storage, only in memory.
[03:10] Tom Becker: network address translation—what do you recommend for egress? NAT gateway vs NAT instances?
[03:18] Marco Rivera: for high-throughput model downloads and updates we recommend NAT Gateways for simplicity and scale, but cost is higher. If you want cost-savvy approach, use NAT64 or a set of autoscaling NAT instances behind a NLB. Also, use VPC endpoints where possible to avoid NAT egress for AWS services.
[03:38] Ben Carter: our team cares about throughput. The runtime uses KV cache heavily—does that generate lots of east-west traffic inside the VPC?
[03:46] Marco Rivera: KV cache is local to the inference process on the node (in-memory) so it doesn't create external network traffic per token. However, if you use a shared KV cache across replicas for long prefixes, that will be RPC traffic between nodes; we use a gRPC-based sharded cache with optional colocated cache nodes in the same subnet to minimize cross-AZ latency.
[04:10] Priya Menon: sharded cache nodes—do they need public IPs?
[04:14] Marco Rivera: no, keep them private. Place them in the same AZ/subnet as the inference nodes to leverage AZ-local networking and avoid inter-AZ replication latency. Use enhanced networking (ENAs) on instances for low-latency RPCs.
[04:28] Lila Park: quick note, for throughput tuning we also recommend instance placement groups when using dedicated capacity to reduce network jitter.
[04:36] Hannah Li: DNS — how do clients discover the model endpoints? we run our own private DNS and don't want split-horizon surprises.
[04:44] Marco Rivera: two options: 1) configure DNS private hosted zone that maps redwood internal hostnames to internal IPs (we can push records via route53 cross-account record sets), or 2) use a bootstrap endpoint in your VPC which the Redwood agent uses to resolve service endpoints via private IPs. PrivateLink simplifies this because the endpoint DNS is provided by AWS and resolves to ENIs in your VPC.
[05:08] Tom Becker: does PrivateLink support cross-account? we have multiple AWS accounts per team.
[05:12] Marco Rivera: yes, PrivateLink supports cross-account access by granting permissions to the service consumer accounts and creating interface endpoints in each account; you manage the endpoint SGs and NACLs locally. For multi-account setups we recommend centralized endpoint management via AWS RAM or terraform modules.
[05:30] Priya Menon: what about VPC peering versus Transit Gateway? which is better for large deployments?
[05:36] Marco Rivera: for a few accounts, VPC peering is fine; for many accounts or central networking, Transit Gateway is preferred. Transit Gateway works well with centralized egress and can attach to multiple VPCs with route propagation, but introduces an extra hop. Latency impact is small if peering/TransitGateway is in same region and configured correctly.
[05:58] Ben Carter: any tips on route tables and security groups?
[06:02] Marco Rivera: keep narrow SGs, allow only necessary ports (gRPC typically 7000-8000 range or 443 if tunneled). For route tables, ensure private subnets have access to NAT or VPC endpoints for artifact pulls. Avoid open 0.0.0.0/0 routes in private subnets.
[06:20] Lila Park: switching to runtime performance—Marco, can you explain how batching and KV cache affect latency and network traffic?
[06:27] Marco Rivera: sure. Batching reduces per-token overhead by combining requests; it primarily affects CPU/GPU scheduling and memory. From network perspective, larger batches mean fewer RPCs but larger payloads — ensure MTU and NLB timeouts are tuned. KV cache reduces compute by serving cached prefixes; if cached locally there's no network impact, but if cache hits require remote shard lookups then you'll see RDMA-like RPCs. So colocate cache shards and inference nodes in same subnets/AZs.
[07:00] Priya Menon: we saw mention of quantization in earlier doc; does quantization change network egress for model weights?
[07:06] Marco Rivera: quantized models are smaller, so downloads and image sizes shrink; good for cold-starts. However, quantized runtime may need different kernels; if using specialized hardware or optimized kernels we ship additional packages which add to artifact size. Plan thin delta updates for quantized-weight patches.
[07:24] Tom Becker: what about TLS/mTLS for node-to-node traffic? we disallow plain text intra-VPC comms by policy.
[07:30] Marco Rivera: we support mTLS for all control and runtime RPCs. Certificates can be managed by Redwood or you can bring your own via S3/SSM or a private CA. We recommend rotating certs regularly and using a short-lived cert model.
[07:48] Hannah Li: logging and audit — how do we capture per-request audit logs without sending PII?
[07:54] Marco Rivera: Redwood runtime can emit structured request logs to a Kinesis or KMS-encrypted S3 endpoint in your account. You control retention and redaction rules. We also support token-level cost traces in the console but those artifacts can be pushed to your logging pipeline rather than Redwood.
[08:12] Ben Carter: are there specific port choices for the inference runtime and management?
[08:16] Marco Rivera: default runtime ports are 7001 for gRPC, 7002 for metrics, and 443/8443 for HTTP tunnels. But you can remap them at install time. Keep SGs narrow to those ports.
[08:30] Lila Park: ok let's talk about the POC: we propose a 2-node inference cluster in your dev VPC, one sharded cache node, and a PrivateLink for control plane. We'll run a baseline latency and throughput benchmark with your sample workload.
[08:44] Priya Menon: sounds good. Benchmarks—what metrics will you capture? p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens?
[08:52] Marco Rivera: yes we'll capture p50/p95/p99, tail latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, network egress, and KV cache hit rate. We'll share a spreadsheet.
[09:02] Tom Becker: about IAM—what roles do you need in our account?
[09:06] Marco Rivera: minimal IAM for provisioning: an instance profile for nodes to pull from S3/ECR, a role for the agent to call control plane via PrivateLink, and optionally a role for KMS decrypt. We'll provide a least-privilege policy.
[09:18] Hannah Li: any known gotchas with route53 cross-account updates? we've had issues with cross-account delegation.
[09:24] Marco Rivera: cross-account record creation requires a role in the DNS account or delegation via a hosted zone association. If you prefer we can provide a CloudFormation stack that your DNS team runs to create the records without cross-account writes.
[09:36] Ben Carter: how about cross-AZ bandwidth costs for large scale KV replication?
[09:40] Marco Rivera: KV replication should be limited; prefer read-local/write-local patterns. If replication is required, co-locate in same AZ or use compression. Cross-AZ bandwidth can add cost; we will surface those in the cost model.
[09:56] Priya Menon: do you support IPv6-only VPCs?
[10:00] Marco Rivera: partial support—control plane may require IPv4 for some features. We can discuss a dual-stack approach.
[10:08] Lila Park: ok let's open for questions from your infra/security folks.
[10:12] Hannah Li: about compliance docs, can you share SOC2 report and pen test summary?
[10:16] Lila Park: yes we will share SOC2 and our security whitepaper; we'll redact sensitive details but provide enough for your legal and security review.
[10:24] Tom Becker: what's the expected time to provision the two-node cluster with our VPC restrictions?
[10:28] Marco Rivera: if we have necessary VPC endpoints and IAM done, we can provision in ~45-60 minutes. If we need image baking and air-gapped artifacts, that adds a day for packing and validation.
[10:40] Ben Carter: for benchmarking, can we run with and without quantization to see tradeoffs?
[10:44] Marco Rivera: absolutely. We'll run three profiles: baseline FP16, quantized int8, and a mixed-precision profile. We'll report latency and quality diffs.
[10:56] Priya Menon: any recommendations on instance types for low-latency inference?
[11:00] Marco Rivera: we recommend A100 or H100 class for high throughput; for latency-sensitive smaller models, an L4 or T4 equivalent can be cost-effective. Also ensure NVMe-backed local storage for cache-heavy workloads.
[11:12] Lila Park: ok wrapping up, recap of next steps and action items.
[11:16] Marco Rivera: I'll prepare an architecture diagram with two deployment options (PrivateLink + managed control plane vs full-in-VPC private runtime) and a runbook for the POC.
[11:24] Lila Park: Lila to share pricing ballpark and the benchmark spreadsheet.
[11:28] Priya Menon: Hannah will validate KMS and compliance needs.
[11:32] Tom Becker: we'll provide a dev account VPC and terraform snippet for the endpoints.
[11:36] Lila Park: perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with artifacts and schedule the POC kickoff.
[11:44] Ben Carter: thanks, that was helpful.
[11:48] Hannah Li: thanks all.
[11:50] END TRANSCRIPT (approx 62 minutes): some transcription artifacts present, occasional speaker mislabels and stutters noted.
